args.body:
MEMORANDUM

TO: Funds & Asset Management Practice Group — Engagement File
FROM: Deal Team
RE: Redline Review — Counterparty Markup of Investment Advisory Agreement
DATE: [Insert Date]

I. INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE

We have been engaged to review the counterparty's redlined markup of the Investment Advisory Agreement (the "Agreement") against our standard form and internal playbook, and to prepare a comprehensive redline review memorandum. This memorandum identifies each material deviation introduced by the counterparty, analyzes the deviation against our standard form, firm precedent, and applicable regulatory framework (including the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, as amended, and applicable rules and guidance thereunder), and sets forth a recommendation to accept, reject, or counter with fallback language.

This memorandum is organized by contract section and flags each deviation with a reference tag (e.g., RL-1, RL-2) for ease of tracking throughout the negotiation. For each deviation, we state: (a) the nature of the change; (b) the deviation versus our standard form and internal playbook; (c) the risk or benefit analysis; and (d) a recommended position.

II. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The counterparty's markup is, in most respects, commercially reasonable but introduces a meaningful number of deviations that shift economic and operational risk away from the counterparty (the investment adviser or the fund client, depending on party) and toward our client. The material themes of the markup are:

1. Broadening of the counterparty's indemnification obligations on our client and narrowing our client's remedy rights (RL-1 through RL-5).
2. Expansion of the representations and warranties and addition of new covenants that exceed market-standard practice (RL-6 through RL-9).
3. Loosening of termination rights and dilution of our client's ability to terminate for cause on short notice (RL-10 through RL-12).
4. Addition of conditions precedent to closing that are outside the operative scope negotiated in the term sheet (RL-13).
5. Revisions to fee and expense provisions, including new cost-shifting and clawback mechanics (RL-14 through RL-16).
6. Conforming and non-material changes that are acceptable as drafted (RL-17).

The most significant bargaining points, warranting escalation to the client and partner review, are the indemnification revisions (RL-1 through RL-5), the termination provisions (RL-10 through RL-12), and the new conditions precedent (RL-13).

III. REVIEW CRITERIA AND METHODOLOGY

We evaluated the counterparty markup against (i) our firm's standard form Investment Advisory Agreement, (ii) our internal playbook for negotiated deviations, and (iii) market practice for comparable funds-asset-management engagements, and (iv) the applicable regulatory framework under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. Each provision was benchmarked for reasonableness, internal consistency, and regulatory compliance.

IV. DEVIATION-BY-DEVIATION ANALYSIS

A. Indemnification Provisions

RL-1 — Counterparty Markup: Broadened Indemnity in Favor of the Counterparty.
Markup Change: The counterparty expanded the carve-outs to our client's indemnification obligation such that our client (the adviser) would indemnify the counterparty for losses "whether or not caused, in whole or in part, by the negligence of the Indemnified Party," and added an additional "including damages arising from the performance of advisory services" catalyst.
Analysis: The standard form limits indemnification to losses arising from a party's gross negligence, willful misconduct, fraud, or a breach of the Agreement. The markup language expands the indemnity to cover ordinary negligence and to sweep in general performance-based damages, which materially broadens our client's exposure and is contrary to our internal playbook, which prohibits adviser indemnification for its own ordinary negligence.
Recommendation: REJECT. Offer counter language restoring the standard gross-negligence/willful-misconduct/fraud/breach causation standard and removing the "whether or not caused by negligence" language.

RL-2 — Counterparty Markup: New Indemnity Cap/Stacking Provision.
Markup Change: The counterparty inserted a provision requiring the indemnifier's liability to be measured without regard to any limitation on fees or aggregate liability elsewhere in the Agreement, effectively "un-capping" the indemnity.
Analysis: This conflicts with the standard form's aggregate liability cap tied to fees earned under the Agreement. Un-capping the indemnity removes the primary commercial protection on the adviser and materially increases downside exposure. This is a major economic deviation.
Recommendation: REJECT. Preserve the fee-based aggregate liability cap, with carve-outs only for fraud and willful misconduct.

RL-3 — Counterparty Markup: Survivability and Extension of Indemnity.
Markup Change: Counterparty extended indemnity survival to a period beyond the standard post-termination survival period and broadened the scope of surviving claims to include matters reasonably expected to arise.
Analysis: The standard form survival period (e.g., three years following termination) is being extended indefinitely. An open-ended or over-broad survival provision is inconsistent with market practice and creates long-tail exposure.
Recommendation: REJECT or Counter. Restore the finite survival period and limit surviving claims to those for which a written claim was made within the survival window.

RL-4 — Counterparty Markup: Defense and Claim-Control Provisions.
Markup Change: Counterparty amended the procedure so that the indemnified party controls defense, settlement, and the selection of counsel, and may settle without the indemnifier's consent so long as the settlement is deemed "in good faith."
Analysis: Standard form gives the indemnifier the right to assume and control the defense and requires the indemnified party's consent to settlements. The markup reverses control of the defense and settlement, exposing our client to settlements it has not approved.
Recommendation: REJECT or Counter. Retain indemnifier control of defense with the mutual reasonable-consent standard for settlement, preserving the standard no-adverse-effect consent carve-outs.

RL-5 — Counterparty Markup: Third-Party Claim Expanding to Direct Claims.
Markup Change: Counterparty expanded indemnification coverage from "third-party claims" to include direct claims between the parties.
Analysis: Indemnification for direct claims is generally disfavored because it is duplicative of breach-of-contract remedies and can circumvent the aggregate liability cap and limitation-of-damages provisions. This conflicts with the standard form and internal playbook.
Recommendation: REJECT. Confirm indemnity applies solely to third-party claims.

B. Representations and Warranties

RL-6 — Counterparty Markup: New Regulatory Compliance Representation.
Markup Change: Counterparty added a new representation that our client's advisory activities comply with the Investment Advisers Act in all respects and that our client maintains all registrations "in good standing with no material deficiencies" — going beyond the standard "where required" formulation.
Analysis: The added "no material deficiencies" language is overbroad and creates a representation that may be untestable and could expose our client to breach based on regulatory observations or deficiencies that are not material or are being remediated. This exceeds market practice.
Recommendation: REJECT or Counter. Modify to the standard "as required by applicable law in all material respects" formulation.

RL-7 — Counterparty Markup: Expanded Accuracy/Update Covenant.
Markup Change: Counterparty added a going-forward covenant requiring our client to update all representations and warranties continuously and to notify the counterparty of any material event within a very short period.
Analysis: Continuous updating of reps is not market practice for an investment advisory agreement and effectively rewrites the rep into an ongoing covenant with an abbreviated notice deadline that may be impractical to satisfy.
Recommendation: REJECT or Counter. Limit updates to closing-date accuracy and, if a notification covenant is included, align the notice period with the standard form.

RL-8 — Counterparty Markup: New Performance/Outcome Representation.
Markup Change: Counterparty inserted a representation that the advisory services will be provided "in accordance with the client's investment objectives and performance expectations."
Analysis: This is a prohibited-form style warranty of performance/outcome. Under the Advisers Act, an adviser cannot guarantee a specific result, and this language could be read as a guarantee. It is inconsistent with the standard form and raises regulatory concerns.
Recommendation: REJECT. Remove; confirm services will be provided in accordance with the Advisers Act fiduciary standard and the Agreement's terms, not an outcome.

RL-9 — Counterparty Markup: Non-Reliance and Sophistication Additions.
Markup Change: Counterparty added mutual non-reliance and sophistication acknowledgments.
Analysis: These additions are generally reasonable and align with market practice and our playbook, provided the wording tracks the standard form. Accept with conforming edits to match the standard form's formulation.
Recommendation: ACCEPT (with conforming edits to match standard form wording).

C. Termination Provisions

RL-10 — Counterparty Markup: Removal of "For Cause" Termination for Adviser Misconduct and Lengthening Notice Periods.
Markup Change: Counterparty deleted our client's right to terminate "for cause" promptly upon an adviser breach, and instead substituted a 90-day notice and cure period for all terminations, including those for fraud or willful misconduct.
Analysis: The standard form permits immediate termination for fraud, willful misconduct, or a material breach without cure. Deleting the cause termination right and imposing a 90-day cure requirement is a material operational deviation that erodes our client's ability to exit promptly in egregious situations. It is inconsistent with the standard form and market practice.
Recommendation: REJECT. Retain immediate for-cause termination for fraud, willful misconduct, and material breach, and retain a shorter (or no-cure) path for those events.

RL-11 — Counterparty Markup: Termination Fee / Amortization Mechanics.
Markup Change: Counterparty inserted a tiered termination fee tied to the remaining term and a new reimbursement obligation for unrecovered setup costs upon termination.
Analysis: While a termination fee is negotiable, the proposed mechanics impose a significant economic penalty and may dilute the "at-will with notice" termination right that is standard in advisory agreements. This is a substantive economic deviation.
Recommendation: COUNTER. If a termination fee is retained, cap it at a reasonable percentage of management fees and eliminate the uncapped reimbursement of setup costs, or remove these provisions entirely to align with the standard form.

RL-12 — Counterparty Markup: Survivability of Termination Provisions and Wind-Down Duties.
Markup Change: Counterparty added an expansive wind-down and transition-services obligation that extends well beyond the termination date and imposes new duties on our client during the run-out period.
Analysis: A transition services obligation is reasonable in moderation, but the markup's scope (including indefinite duration and inclusion of client-facing activities) exceeds the standard form. This creates ongoing operational obligations that should be clearly bounded.
Recommendation: COUNTER. Limit the wind-down/transition period to a finite run-out and limit the scope to the transfer of books and records and reasonably requested transition assistance.

D. Conditions Precedent

RL-13 — Counterparty Markup: New Conditions Precedent to Closing.
Markup Change: Counterparty added new conditions to closing, including the delivery of independent legal opinions, evidence of regulatory no-action or guidance, and satisfaction of a material-adverse-effect condition with no carve-out for market conditions.
Analysis: The terms sheet and pre-markup standard form did not contemplate these closing conditions. Adding a MAE condition and requiring legal opinions and regulatory evidence imposes new pre-closing burdens and delays closing, and in some respects conflicts with the negotiated commercial deal. This exceeds the agreed scope.
Recommendation: REJECT or COUNTER. Remove the new conditions not contemplated by the term sheet; if closing conditions are needed, limit them to those in the standard form and carve out market fluctuations from any MAE condition.

E. Fees and Expenses

RL-14 — Counterparty Markup: New Expense Cap and Cost-Shifting.
Markup Change: Counterparty added a provision sharing or shifting certain expenses (including regulatory compliance costs and audit costs) to our client, and imposed a cap on the counterparty's reimbursable expenses.
Analysis: The allocation of ordinary operating and compliance costs is a negotiated commercial point. Shifting compliance costs shifts regulatory burden pricing to our client in a way not in the standard form. This is a deviation to address as a commercial matter.
Recommendation: COUNTER. Confirm that our client's fee is inclusive of ordinary advisory costs per the standard form; if additional cost allocations are required, align with market ranges and clarify which costs are borne by whom.

RL-15 — Counterparty Markup: Modification of Fee Basis / Calculation Methodology.
Markup Change: Counterparty modified the management fee calculation methodology (e.g., changing the valuation date and adding a look-through to underlying fund assets).
Analysis: Changes to the fee basis are material commercial deviations. The change to a look-through methodology and altered valuation dates could affect the fee compute and requires client and commercial review.
Recommendation: COUNTER. Confirm the fee methodology matches the term sheet; retain the standard valuation date and fee accrual methodology absent client approval of a change.

RL-16 — Counterparty Markup: Clawback / True-Up Provision.
Markup Change: Counterparty added a clawback/true-up provision under which our client would be required to return fees upon a subsequent adjustment.
Analysis: A true-up on final valuation is reasonable if it reconciles against actual performance/valuation; however, the markup's unilateral clawback without an offsetting right to additional fees in the event of an upward adjustment is asymmetrical.
Recommendation: COUNTER or ACCEPT with revision. Make any true-up mutual and tied to final audited figures.

F. Other / Conforming

RL-17 — Counterparty Markup: Conforming and Non-Material Changes.
Markup Change: Various conforming edits, defined-term harmonization, and administrative changes.
Analysis: These are immaterial and consistent with the standard form's intent.
Recommendation: ACCEPT.

V. REGULATORY CONSIDERATIONS

As this is an investment advisory agreement, the redline must be considered against the Advisers Act of 1940, including the antifraud provisions of Section 206, the adviser's fiduciary duty, and applicable SEC rules and interpretive guidance. Two flagged deviations present notable regulatory considerations: (a) RL-8, the performance/outcome representation, which risks an impermissible guarantee of results and on which we have recommended a REJECT; and (b) the continued appropriateness of the fee arrangements (RL-14 through RL-16) in light of the duty to ensure fees are not excessive and are adequately disclosed. We also confirm that no provision in the markup requires our client to waive or limit its fiduciary duties under the Advisers Act.

VI. RECOMMENDED NEGOTIATING POSITION

We recommend the following overall posture:

1. REJECT the material risk-shifting deviations in the indemnification (RL-1 through RL-5) and termination (RL-10 through RL-12) provisions, and offer counter-language consistent with the standard form.
2. REJECT the new conditions precedent (RL-13) and the performance/outcome representation (RL-8), as these are either out of agreed scope or raise regulatory concerns.
3. REJECT or counter the representation expansions (RL-6, RL-7) to standard form formulations.
4. COUNTER the fee and expense deviations (RL-14 through RL-16) as commercial matters requiring client input.
5. ACCEPT the conforming and reasonable provisions (RL-9, RL-17), with conforming edits to standard form wording.

VII. OPEN ITEMS AND NEXT STEPS

- Confirm with the client the commercial posture on fee allocation and termination-fee economics (RL-11, RL-14, RL-15, RL-16).
- Obtain partner sign-off on the recommended positions before the next round of comments.
- Prepare a clean markup reflecting the recommended accept/reject/counter positions for issuance to counterparty, together with this memorandum.

This memorandum is a privilege-protected work product of the Funds & Asset Management practice group and is prepared in anticipation of litigation or the negotiation of the Agreement. It is intended solely for the use of the engagement team and client.

[Signature / Deal Team]
